title: Income-tax repeal
summary: Repeals the planned 9.9% tax on Washington taxable income above $1 million and prohibits income-measured state/local taxes. [AG explanation]
currentLaw: The 2026 law taxes 2028 income, with first payments in 2029. Couples share the $1 million deduction. Five percent goes to Fair Start for Kids; the remainder to the general fund. [AG explanation; Enacted law]
yes: Repeal the tax and adopt the broader income-tax prohibition.
no: Keep the 2026 tax law and its scheduled collections.
history: March 2026: Legislature enacted ESSB 6346; governor signed March 30. [Enacted law]

tradeoffs.label: Supporters' argument
tradeoffs.text: Avoid a new tax, protect investment and prevent expansion below today's threshold. [Campaign arguments]

tradeoffs.label: Opponents' argument
tradeoffs.text: Retain service funding and ask high earners to contribute more. [Campaign arguments]

tradeoffs.label: Where revenue goes
tradeoffs.text: No fixed education share or district-specific return is mandated. School-meal language states legislative intent. [Enacted law]

fiscal: OFM's July ballot estimate: $11.432 billion less revenue in SFY2027–31, including $377 million less Fair Start funding; $150.47 million net agency savings. [OFM fiscal statement]
caveat: AG says accompanying non-income-tax credits and exemptions survive repeal. Particular service cuts depend on later budgets. Campaign $13 billion claims use a different figure than the official ballot estimate.

title: Parental rights in public schools
summary: Restores the 2024 parental-rights list in RCW 28A.605.005, reversing its 2025 revisions. [House summary]
currentLaw: Parents already have materials access and sex-education opt-outs. Education-record requests generally allow up to 45 days, with separate health/privacy rules. [Current law]
yes: Restore broader school-record access, 10-business-day requests and medical-service notices. [Proposal]
no: Keep the revised 2025 rights list and privacy provisions. [Current law]
history: 2025: HB 1296 revised its rights list. [House summary]
2026: Legislature took no action; initiative proceeds to voters. [House summary]

tradeoffs.label: Supporters' argument
tradeoffs.text: Faster access and medical notices strengthen family involvement and school trust. [Campaign arguments]

tradeoffs.label: Opponents' argument
tradeoffs.text: Broader disclosure and narrower abuse exceptions could endanger vulnerable students or deter counseling. [Campaign arguments]

tradeoffs.label: Legal distinction
tradeoffs.text: Rewrites one statute, not all HB 1296. Separate employee-abuse notification and teacher protections remain. [Proposal; Separate abuse-notice law; Teacher protections]

fiscal: OFM: no state fiscal or revenue effect; local policy-update costs may be minor but are indeterminate. [OFM fiscal statement]
caveat: No explicit pronoun/gender-change reporting clause. Broader records access may disclose sensitive information. Removing rights from this list does not itself repeal independent protections.

title: Girls' school-sports eligibility
summary: Restricts covered female-only school competitions and requires healthcare-provider sex verification. [House summary]
currentLaw: WIAA rule 18.16.0 allows participation consistent with gender identity. [WIAA handbook]
yes: Exclude students defined as biologically male from girls' competitions; require female-category athletes to provide medical verification. [Proposal]
no: Keep current eligibility rules without this new verification mandate.
history: 2025: Filed as an initiative to the Legislature. [House summary]
2026: Legislature took no action; proposal proceeds to voters. [House summary]

tradeoffs.label: Supporters' argument
tradeoffs.text: Sex-based eligibility protects fairness, safety and female athletes' opportunities. [Campaign arguments]

tradeoffs.label: Opponents' argument
tradeoffs.text: Excludes transgender girls and adds privacy, access and participation barriers for female-category athletes. [Campaign arguments]

tradeoffs.label: Scope
tradeoffs.text: Covered K–12 interschool competitions, including participating private schools; not a general college, recreation or PE ban. [House summary; Proposal]

fiscal: OFM: approximately $21,000 one-time state guidance cost; local rule-update costs indeterminate; no revenue effect. [OFM fiscal statement]
caveat: Requires verification using listed biological criteria but specifies no particular exam, test or hormone threshold. Claims that invasive exams are certain—or existing records always suffice—go beyond explicit text. [Proposal]

title: Seattle Transit Measure
scope: City of Seattle · includes Queen Anne
summary: Replaces the expiring transit sales tax with authority for up to 0.3% for up to ten years, supporting transit service, access and related projects. [Official ballot explanation]
currentLaw: The current 0.15% transit sales tax, approved in 2020, expires March 31, 2027. [Official ballot explanation]
yes: Authorize the city to enact a replacement transit tax, no earlier than April 1, 2027. [Ordinance 127474]
no: Reject this replacement; the existing transit tax still expires. Other transit funding remains, but this city supplement would end without another funding decision.
history: 2020: Voters approved the current six-year transit tax. [Official ballot explanation]
July 21, 2026: Council passed the replacement measure unanimously. [Council announcement]

tradeoffs.label: Supporters' argument
tradeoffs.text: More frequent buses, later/weekend service and more subsidized ORCA passes improve access while reducing car dependence. [Yes campaign]

tradeoffs.label: Opponents' argument
tradeoffs.text: Doubling this sales-tax component burdens household budgets; improve spending accountability and fare collection first. [Pamphlet opposition]

tradeoffs.label: Oversight
tradeoffs.text: Transit Advisory Board oversight and annual/midterm reporting are required. [Official ballot explanation]

fiscal: City estimate: approximately $138 million annually. The component rises from 15¢ to 30¢ per $100 of taxable purchases if the full rate is enacted—an added 15¢. [Council announcement; arithmetic]
caveat: The proposition grants taxing authority; a future ordinance enacts the tax. Household-cost and service-expansion estimates depend on spending and implementation. This is separate from Seattle's 2024 property-tax transportation levy.
